title: Multiplying Matrices
short: Each entry is a row times a column.
trouble: Students multiply matching entries, or assume AB = BA.

blocks.html: Adding matrices works entry by entry, so you might expect multiplying to work the same way. It does not. The useful product combines a row of the first matrix with a column of the second, and it comes from real calculations like totals and costs.

If $A$ is $m \times n$ and $B$ is $n \times p$, then $AB$ is $m \times p$, and its entry in row $i$, column $j$ is row $i$ of $A$ times column $j$ of $B$: multiply matching entries and add. The inside sizes must match. In general $AB \ne BA$.

Suppose row $1$ of $A$ lists what you buy: $2$ apples and $3$ pears. Column $1$ of $B$ lists the prices at a store: $\$1$ and $\$2$. Your bill there is $2 \cdot 1 + 3 \cdot 2 = 8$: a row times a column. Each other entry of $AB$ is another shopper at another store. The row and the column must have the same length, or the items do not line up. Swapping the order asks a different question, so $BA$ is usually different.

blocks.cap: The matrix times the vector $\mathbf{v}$: each entry of $A\mathbf{v}$ is a row of $A$ times $\mathbf{v}$. Edit the entries and drag $\mathbf{v}$.

blocks.title: Different sizes
steps: $(2 \times 3)(3 \times 2)$: the inside sizes match, and the product is $2 \times 2$.

blocks.title: Order matters
blocks.q: With $A$ and $B$ from the first example, find $BA$.
steps: Row 1 of $B$ times the columns of $A$: $5 \cdot 1 + 0 \cdot 3 = 5$ and $5 \cdot 2 + 0 \cdot 4 = 10$.

blocks.html: Multiplying matching entries, as if $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 5 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ were $\begin{bmatrix} 5 & 0 \\ -3 & 8 \end{bmatrix}$, or assuming $AB = BA$. Check the sizes first (inside numbers equal, outside numbers give the answer's size), then compute every entry as a row times a column.
